prompt:
A MergeStream Continuous Delivery Pipeline Engine system with main features including local Git repository monitoring, automated branch merging, shell-based test execution, role-governed project management, in-app notification delivery, and comprehensive audit logging.

MergeStream serves small development teams of three to fifteen engineers who operate entirely on local infrastructure without any external service dependency. The React-based single-page application presents a central dashboard where every registered project displays its latest pipeline health through intuitive color-coded indicators — green for passed, red for failed, and amber for merge conflicts. The interface refreshes pipeline state via short polling at five-second intervals, giving developers a near-real-time view of build activity. Three distinct roles govern the experience: Administrators manage all users and projects, Maintainers configure pipeline settings such as repository filesystem path, target branch, test command, polling interval (configurable from ten to sixty seconds), and automatic retry attempts up to three on test failure, while Developers trigger builds and browse results. A scrollable pipeline history view per project surfaces the most recent fifty runs with expandable log output, and a dedicated merge conflict viewer renders conflicting file paths alongside raw diff content so engineers can diagnose issues without leaving the browser. An in-app notification center alerts users when their branch encounters merge conflicts or test failures, tracking unread and read status per message and automatically pruning entries beyond two hundred per user. The Administrator panel provides user creation, password resets, role assignment, and a searchable audit trail of the last one thousand system events covering logins, pipeline triggers, and configuration changes, with each entry timestamped in MM/DD/YYYY 12-hour format.

On the server side, the Express backend persists all data in MongoDB, storing documents for users, projects, pipeline runs, notifications, and audit events. User passwords are hashed with bcrypt, and accounts lock for fifteen minutes after five consecutive failed login attempts. JWT-based session tokens are issued at login with a configurable expiration of eight hours, and a refresh mechanism allows seamless re-authentication without re-entering credentials. Role-based access control enforces menu visibility, data scope, and action-level permissions — for instance, Developers cannot modify project settings, and only Administrators can deactivate or delete accounts. The pipeline engine polls bare Git repositories on the local filesystem, detects new commits on feature branches, and attempts an automated merge into the configured target branch. Conflicts are captured with file paths and line numbers, while successful merges proceed to shell-based test execution whose stdout and stderr output is stored up to two megabytes per run. Pipeline statuses progress through Queued, Running, Passed, Failed, Conflict, or Cancelled, with a maximum of four concurrent executions and a FIFO overflow queue holding up to fifty pending jobs. Build history retains five hundred runs per project before automatic pruning. All sensitive fields such as hashed passwords and token payloads are masked in API responses and audit logs. Input validation guards every endpoint against injection attacks, and CSRF protections secure state-changing operations. A standardized RESTful API layer with consistent error codes and idempotent write operations connects the React frontend to Express, ensuring a cleanly decoupled architecture where every interaction flows through documented JSON endpoints — all running on a single local server with zero internet requirement.
